summary: Gives guidelines for implementors and users on running OSPF over frame relay networks. Frame relay links connect many routers without behaving like a simple broadcast network, so careful configuration is needed. It is informational and does not define a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1586 explains why OSPF was awkward to run over frame relay and what to configure instead. The answer is to treat each virtual circuit as its own point-to-point link, so that routers no longer all have to be wired to each other, and to give each circuit its own cost so that traffic takes the best one.

subtitle: How to configure OSPF over frame relay so that a full mesh of virtual circuits is not needed.

tldr.problem: OSPF treats a frame relay network as a non-broadcast multiple access link, which means every router must have a virtual circuit to every other router, and the cost of that grows with the square of the number of routers.
tldr.mechanism: The memo asks for OSPF implementations to support logical interfaces inside a physical one, so that one virtual circuit can be a logical point-to-point link and a group of them a logical NBMA network, each with its own link metric.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that specifies no standard of any kind. Its recommendations need no change to the protocol itself, only to how routers are built and configured.

It asks for configuration and implementation changes rather than protocol changes, and its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in it.

sections.title: Why Frame Relay Was Hard for OSPF
sections.content:
A frame relay network provides virtual circuits, VCs, to interconnect attached devices. Each VC is uniquely identified at each frame relay interface by a Data Link Connection Identifier, a DLCI, and RFC 1294 specifies the encapsulation of multiprotocol traffic over frame relay. The devices on a frame relay network may either be fully interconnected with a mesh of VCs, or partially interconnected.

OSPF characterises frame relay networks as non-broadcast multiple access, NBMA, because they can support more than two attached routers but do not have a broadcast capability. Under that model, the physical frame relay interface on a router corresponds to a single OSPF interface through which the router is connected to one or more neighbours on the frame relay network, and all the neighbouring routers must also be directly connected to each other over the frame relay network. It follows that OSPF implementations using the NBMA model for frame relay do not work when the routers are partially interconnected.

The memo then identifies two separate problems with that. First, the number of VCs required for full-mesh connectivity increases quadratically with the number of routers. Public frame relay services typically offer performance guarantees for each VC provisioned by the service, which means real physical resources in the frame relay network are devoted to each VC, and for this the customer eventually pays. The expense of full-mesh connectivity therefore grows quadratically with the number of interconnected routers, and the memo says plainly that OSPF implementations are needed that allow partial connectivity over frame relay.

Second, using a single link metric, per type of service, for the frame relay interface does not allow OSPF to weigh some VCs more heavily than others according to the performance characteristics of each connection. To make efficient use of the frame relay network resources, it should be possible to assign different link metrics to different VCs.

These limitations become more severe as the network size increases, and they render frame relay technology less cost effective than it could be for large networks. The solutions the memo proposes do not increase complexity by much and do not require any changes to the OSPF protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Frame relay gives you a set of private lines between routers, billed one by one. OSPF assumed that on such a network every router could see every other router, so it wanted a private line to each of them. That is fine for three routers and expensive for thirty.

sections.title: The Recommendations in Brief
sections.content:
The first recommendation is to expand the general view of an OSPF interface to account for its functional type, point-to-point, broadcast or NBMA, rather than its physical type. In most instances the physical network can only serve one function and can only be defined as one type of OSPF interface. For multiplexed interfaces such as frame relay, however, logical connections between routers can serve different functions, so one VC on a frame relay interface can be viewed distinctly from other VCs on the same physical interface.

The solution therefore requires that OSPF be able to support logical interfaces, that is, logical networks, as well as physical interfaces. Each logical network can be either point-to-point, a single VC, or NBMA, a collection of VCs. It is not necessary to define new interface types for logical networks, since the operation of the protocol over logical point-to-point networks and logical NBMA networks remains the same as for the corresponding physical networks. Logical point-to-point links, for instance, could be numbered or unnumbered. It is only necessary for implementations to provide the hooks that give users the ability to configure an individual VC as a logical point-to-point network, or a collection of VCs as a logical NBMA network.

The memo is careful to record the other side of the trade-off. The NBMA model does provide some economy in OSPF protocol processing and overhead, and it is the recommended mode of operation for small homogeneous networks. Other than the designated router and the backup designated router, each router maintains only two adjacencies, one each with the DR and the BDR, regardless of the size of the NBMA network. When frame relay VCs are configured as point-to-point links, a router would have many more adjacencies to maintain, resulting in increased protocol overhead. If all the VCs had comparable performance characteristics as well, there might not be compelling reasons to assign a different link metric to each VC.
sections.plainLanguage: The change is to think of the interface type as a property of each virtual circuit rather than of the physical card. One circuit can be a plain point-to-point link to one neighbour, and several circuits can be grouped into a shared network. The price is more adjacencies to maintain.

sections.title: Configuring Numbered Logical Interfaces
sections.content:
The memo describes how an administrator would configure numbered logical interfaces over frame relay, in four steps.

In the first step the physical interface is configured, specifying the relevant parameters such as the slot, connector and port numbers, the physical frame format, the encoding and the clock mode. In its internal interface MIB the router should create a new ifEntry in the ifTable, assign the physical interface an ifIndex, and increment the ifNumber by one.

In the second step the data link layer over the interface is configured, specifying frame relay as the encapsulation method, and parameters such as the DLCI encoding type and length, the maximum frame size, the management interface, Annex D LMI, and the address resolution procedure, manual or inverse ARP. If a management interface is not supported, frame relay VCs must be configured manually.

In the third step the IP network layer is configured for the interface, by specifying the number of logical interfaces and the IP address and subnet mask for each numbered logical interface, and the VCs, by DLCI, associated with each logical network interface where there is more than one. If an address resolution protocol such as inverse ARP is being used, it should suffice to specify a list of IP addresses for the frame relay interface and have inverse ARP create the DLCI and IP address binding.

In the fourth step OSPF is configured to run over each logical interface as appropriate, specifying the necessary interface parameters such as the area ID, the link metric, the protocol timers and intervals, the designated router priority, and the list of neighbours for the designated router. OSPF interfaces consisting of one VC can be treated as point-to-point links, while multi-VC OSPF interfaces are treated as NBMA subnets. In its internal OSPF MIB the router should create additional entries in the ospfIfTable, each with the appropriate ospfIfType, nbma or pointTopoint.
sections.plainLanguage: The configuration follows the stack from the bottom up. Set up the physical port, then frame relay on it, then the IP addresses of the logical links inside it, and finally tell OSPF which of those links to run on and what they should cost.

sections.title: Numbered or Unnumbered Logical Interfaces
sections.content:
OSPF uses the IP address to instance each numbered interface. Since an unnumbered point-to-point link has no IP address, the ifIndex from the interface MIB is used instead. That is straightforward for a physical point-to-point network, because the ifIndex is assigned when the interface is configured. Logical interfaces over frame relay, however, do not have distinct and unique values for ifIndex.

To allow OSPF to instance unnumbered logical point-to-point links, it would be necessary to assign each such link a unique ifIndex in the third configuration step. The memo notes that this could lead to some confusion in the interfaces table, since a new ifTable entry would have to be created for each logical point-to-point link, and that this departure from the standard practice of creating interface table entries only for physical interfaces could be viewed as an unnecessary complication.

Alternatively, it is possible to build a private MIB that contains data structures to instance unnumbered logical links, but making recommendations for the structure and use of such a private MIB is beyond the scope of this work. Even if unnumbered logical point-to-point links were implemented in this manner, it would still be necessary to allow a frame relay interface to be configured with multiple IP addresses when a router is connected to multiple NBMA subnets through a single physical interface. So, while it is possible to define unnumbered logical point-to-point links in OSPF, the memo finds this alternative less attractive than using numbered logical point-to-point links.
sections.plainLanguage: A logical link could be left without an IP address, but then it needs a separate entry in the router's interface table, and the memo judges that messier than simply giving each one an address.

sections.title: Designing the Network
sections.content:
The ability to configure distinct logical interfaces over frame relay gives users a great deal of flexibility in designing frame relay networks for use with OSPF. Because routers can be partially interconnected over frame relay, it is possible to design networks more cost-effectively than before.

The memo lists the issues to consider: the price and cost structure for VCs, which may be fixed, distance-sensitive or banded, and for ports; the performance guarantees provided; traffic distribution, local or long-haul; and protocol efficiency. It repeats that the NBMA model provides some economy in OSPF protocol processing and overhead and is recommended for small homogeneous networks.

In general, users should configure their networks to contain several small NBMA clusters, which are in turn interconnected by long-haul VCs. The best choices for the number of routers in each cluster and the size of the long-haul logical point-to-point links depend on the factors just listed. If it is necessary to architect a more flat network, the ability to assign different link metrics to different groups of VCs allows for greater efficiency in using frame relay resources, since VCs with better performance characteristics, in throughput and delay, could be assigned lower link metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: The advice for a network designer is to build clusters: a handful of routers wired together in a mesh, and the clusters joined by long-haul links. That keeps the mesh small while the distance between sites is carried by a circuit that is cheap to provision.

sections.title: Conclusion and Security
sections.content:
The memo concludes that it has specified guidelines for OSPF implementors and users to bring about improvements in how the protocol runs over frame relay networks, that these recommendations do not require any protocol changes, and that they allow for simpler, more efficient and cost-effective network designs. The recommendation is that OSPF implementations be able to support logical interfaces, each consisting of one or more virtual circuits and used as numbered logical point-to-point links for one VC, or as logical NBMA networks for more than one VC, and that the current NBMA model for frame relay should continue to be used for small homogeneous networks consisting of a few routers.

The Security Considerations section is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. The acknowledgements record that the memo is the result of work done in the OSPF Working Group of the IETF, and that comments and contributions from several sources are included, naming Fred Baker of ACC, John Moy of Proteon and Bala Rajagopalan of AT&T Bell Laboratories.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing in the protocol has to change; the routers just have to be able to see inside the interface and be told which circuits to use. The memo says nothing about security.

viz.caption: THE TWO WAYS TO RUN OSPF OVER A FRAME RELAY INTERFACE

left.title: Logical NBMA
left.desc: Must be full-mesh connected. Each router keeps only two adjacencies, one to the designated router and one to the backup designated router, whatever the size of the network.

right.title: Logical point-to-point
right.desc: Routers may be only partly interconnected, and each VC can carry its own link metric, but a router keeps an adjacency for every VC it has, which raises protocol overhead.

cells: 1. Physical interface
Slot, connector and port numbers, physical frame format, encoding and clock mode; a new ifEntry in the ifTable, an ifIndex, and ifNumber incremented by one.
2. Data link layer
Frame relay encapsulation, the DLCI encoding type and length, maximum frame size, the Annex D management interface, and the address resolution procedure, manual or inverse ARP.
3. IP network layer
The number of logical interfaces, and the IP address and subnet mask for each, with the DLCIs of each group where there is more than one.
4. OSPF
Area ID, link metric, protocol timers and intervals, designated router priority and the neighbour list, with new ospfIfTable entries typed nbma or pointTopoint.
